summary: This document proposes a framework for managing the LISP Endpoint Identifier address block, relying on hierarchical distribution where requesting organizations are granted temporary use of prefixes. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: This explained how the special address range for LISP would be handed out in small pieces to organizations, for a limited time. It is now historic.

subtitle: How to register and manage IPv6 prefixes from the LISP EID address block

tldr.problem: The LISP EID block (2001:5::/32) allocated in RFC 7954 requires a management framework so that organizations deploying LISP can request and temporarily use sub-prefixes for their experiments in a fair and organized way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7955 establishes a registration policy where organizations request EID prefixes through a standardized template, RIPE NCC maintains a public registry of allocations, renewals occur annually, and all registrations expire when the experimental period ends unless the IETF decides to make LISP permanent.
tldr.outcome: LISP sites can request prefixes from the EID block on a first-come, first-served basis, with the registry ensuring fairness, accountability, and public visibility of all allocations. The document is now historic.

today: RFC 7955 is Historic. RIPE NCC managed the LISP EID block registry during the experimental period, which ended in August 2019 when the allocation was not made permanent.

sections.title: Managing the LISP EID Block
sections.content:
RFC 7954 allocated a /32 IPv6 prefix (2001:5::/32) for use as the global Endpoint Identifier (EID) space for LISP experimentation. This RFC provides the management framework for distributing and administering that address block. The framework allows organizations and individuals to request temporary allocations of EID prefixes from the reserved block for their LISP deployments and experiments.

The Locator/ID Separation Protocol separates the identity of a computer (EID) from its location (Routing Locator, RLOC). Rather than allocating entire organizations' own IP address ranges for use as EIDs, this framework provides a hierarchical distribution mechanism. A centralized registry manager (RIPE NCC) grants organizations exclusive temporary use of sub-prefixes from the /32, ensuring all allocations are unique and preventing conflicts.
sections.eli5: This document explains how organizations would get pieces of the special LISP address range and use them for a limited time. A registry kept track of who had which pieces.

sections.title: Registration Policy for EID Prefixes
sections.content:
Organizations requesting EID prefixes must follow the registration policy outlined in the RFC. Prefixes are made available on a temporary basis for experimental uses only. When requesting a prefix, the organization must provide a short description of the intended experiment or deployment. The registration period is 12 months, and registrations must be renewed regularly to ensure active use. A renewal should not cause a change in the previously allocated prefix, providing continuity for ongoing experiments.

When a registration expires and is removed from the registry, reuse of that prefix by a different organization is avoided where possible, with a minimum delay of at least one week between removal and reuse. This prevents confusion and allows time for network changes to propagate. When the experimental period for the entire EID block expires (August 2019, or August 2022 if extended), all EID prefix registrations expire automatically. If the IETF decides to terminate the experiment, all prefixes must be released and returned to the free pool.
sections.eli5: Organizations request small pieces of the LISP address range for experiments. They keep their piece for 12 months, then renew if they want to continue. When everyone is done, all the addresses get returned.

sections.title: What Organizations Must Provide
sections.content:
All EID prefix registrations must satisfy several requirements. First, each registered EID prefix must be globally unique within the registry. Second, all registration information must be collected and made publicly available through interfaces that allow both searching for specific registrations and browsing the entire registry. Third, the registry operator must permit organizations holding registered EID prefixes to delegate those prefixes in the reverse DNS space, enabling proper DNS resolution for their LISP endpoints.

Finally, anyone can obtain an entry in the registry by understanding that the prefix is exclusively for use in the LISP experimental network and that their registration details will be openly published. The RFC emphasizes that transparency and accountability are central to the framework—there is no hard limit to the number of registrations an organization can submit, but all details must be accurate and publicly visible. The registrations include organization information, contact details, prefix specifications, and descriptions of the proposed LISP experiment or deployment.
sections.eli5: Each piece of the address range must be unique and public. Organizations must provide contact information and explain what they plan to do with their addresses. Everything is listed in a public registry.

sections.title: The Request Template and Information Required
sections.content:
The RFC provides a standardized request template that organizations must use when applying for EID prefixes. Organizations provide their name, address, phone number, and website (or leave this section empty if an individual is requesting). The contact person information includes name, address, phone, optional fax, and email.

For the prefix request itself, organizations specify the desired prefix size (expressed as an address prefix length), the rationale for that size, and a lease period. The RFC notes that all registrations expire on the earlier of 12 months from registration or August 2019. The most important part of the request is the experiment description, where organizations detail their LISP deployment or experiment, explain interoperability with existing LISP deployments, and describe how they will interoperate with the legacy non-LISP Internet. Organizations can optionally provide reverse DNS server information for their prefix.
sections.eli5: Organizations fill out a form with their contact information, how much of the address range they need, why they need it, and what they plan to do with it. They submit this to the registry manager.

sections.title: RIPE NCC as Registry Manager
sections.content:
IANA designated RIPE NCC as the operational manager of the LISP EID block registry for the duration of the experimental allocation. Registration is on a first-come, first-served basis, with RIPE NCC accepting requests that satisfy the policies and requirements outlined in the RFC. RIPE NCC makes all received requests publicly available through its registry interface.

RIPE NCC provides the registration service, maintains the public request forms that include at least the information from the standard template, and manages the registry according to the policy defined in RFC 7955. While the RFC does not suggest a minimum allocation size, RIPE NCC may introduce such a minimum for management purposes. The RFC emphasizes that this arrangement has no IANA actions required; RIPE NCC operates under the experimental allocation policy for the duration of the experiment (August 2019, or optionally August 2022).
sections.eli5: RIPE NCC, a real internet registry, kept the list of who had which LISP addresses. They accepted requests in the order they came in and published the list so everyone could see who had what.
